summary:
Erzurum province sits wholly inside Türkiye's national legal framework; no separate provincial regime applies to trans visitors, and the criminal code, civil code, Health Ministry regulations and police practice operating in Istanbul or Ankara operate identically here.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 under onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protection of "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures including longer sentences for children and online-content removal. The draft had not been enacted as reported, and authorities have in places acted as though its prohibitions were already in force.

The baseline legal position is less restrictive than the enforcement environment suggests. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the same year gender-reassignment surgery was legalised. A court action to close the Lambda Istanbul association was overruled by the Constitutional Court, which kept the organisation open.

Recognition stops there. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not recognised; LGBT people are barred from serving openly in the military; and no comprehensive national law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Türkiye 47th of 49 countries.

Street-level policing is the immediate hazard for a visitor. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any stop is an occasion on which a passport is compared against presentation.

Lethal violence is documented and the state response is asymmetric. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 43 of them taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with trans people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest.

Pride events remain flashpoints nationwide. Pride has been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. Poyraz, a transgender prisoner, was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation after accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers described a prolonged medical delay, prosecutors entering the prison two days later and witness statements going untaken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.
tangentialFactors:
The pending draft package has functioned ahead of enactment: reporting on the 2025 Istanbul stops records a detained woman stating that no fines were imposed but that she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was applied to her. Foreign visitors face the same pattern of documentation without charge at identity checkpoints.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees across Türkiye are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners; there is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the depth of the pattern rather than as a statement of current law.

The Erdoğan government's framing of its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals" is identified by Human Rights Watch as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma, and the same language runs through the draft package's provisions.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Türkiye since 1988, alongside legal gender-reassignment surgery since the same year, and the Constitutional Court has intervened to keep an LGBT association open after a closure action against Lambda Istanbul.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex partnerships or joint adoption, and no route to open military service; these gaps shape employment, housing and family life for LGBT people living in Erzurum.

The Health Ministry's September 2025 regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that preceded it affect how gender-related care is recorded and reported for residents as well as visitors, with "gender reassignment" now an official category on medical-board reports and the "other" option barred.

Kaos GL's 2025 reporting indicates that detention and ill-treatment have become routine rather than exceptional for LGBT residents, with 89 torture or ill-treatment cases recorded in that year against 51 the year before.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory reports policing, healthcare access, detention or violence specifically in Erzurum; the province-level record is assembled entirely from national and Istanbul-based material, and the Erzurum reference itself yielded no usable finding. Local conditions in Erzurum remain unresolved on this record.

The 11th Judicial Package provisions described here were reported as a leaked draft and had not been enacted when last sourced; whether any provision has since been passed is unresolved.

The claimed scope of Article 5 European Convention on Human Rights violations rests on legal experts cited in reporting rather than a court ruling, and no judicial finding on those GBT checks is sourced.

Accounts of the Sincan Women's Prison death, including the medical delay and the absence of witness statements, derive from other trans prisoners, visiting lawyers and rights groups; no independent investigation outcome is available, and the case's status after the December 2025 parliamentary question is unresolved.
